quotes.text: Withdraw only from the hand that empties on clear mornings.
Forgive the empty hand twice; close the gate slowly on the third; reopen at the first trickle.
Send a trickle, never nothing, to the thrice-empty hand — nothing closes the gate, and closed gates rust shut.
But the instant water returns from his side — not half, not the floor, only *some* — open wide the next morning.
He raged, and the next dawn sent nothing.
"Why patience?" asked the fox, who had argued every season for the single great theft.
To the taker, a trickle — never nothing, never a seal.
So the ladder was recut, and the five rungs read:
"The river takes its toll, not my neighbor."
The extra sliver is not charity — it is rent on his courage.
"Why not nothing?" asked the merchants who had waited out the mist their whole lives.
A young ferryman asked, "What if nothing comes at all?"

note: From 'close only against the repeatedly empty hand' to a trickle never nothing; fox argues for the great theft and goes hungry.

quotes.text: Forgive once freely, twice gladly, and only then grow careful.
and only after three winters call a neighbor false.
When a pattern hardens, shrink by halves — never to nothing.
Close slowly, and reopen the instant a stream returns.
He cursed his partner, sealed his granary, and sent nothing ever after.
The Fox said, "Mark him in the ledger with a black stone."
"I will send all five," he said, "because my gate is not a reply. It is a declaration.
*The river lies, but the hand does not.*
Open the hand first; the gate opens only from your side.
Return more than half to the one who risked all; half to the careful stranger.
"You are a fool," said the Fox, "and the ledger proves it."
Had I returned six, his daring would have earned him one fruit more than cowardice.

note: Grow careful after two forgivenesses, then shrink by halves never to nothing; R10 sends all five to a silent shore.

quotes.text: "Then send a little less, but never nothing.
"Then send a little less, but never nothing. A closed river feeds no one
An empty crossing may be the fog. Two may be the fog. By the third, step back
And when the answering spark comes, open wide again, at once, without a word about the past.
Vela shouted the same, and both ferried nothing, and both grew thin on a river heavy with wealth.
**To the thrice-empty hand, a trickle — never nothing.**
**The Four Weights of Ilva's Scale**
the mist steals, but it cannot steal intention.
"Half is the floor, not the roof," said Ilva.
A young man objected: "But some will take and never give."
for someone must move first, and it costs you almost nothing to be that one.

note: Consistent 'less but never nothing' rule refined with patience counts, testing basket, four weights and a ladder.

quotes.text: Only then did he close his channel — not in rage, but as a farmer closes a gate on a field that will not grow.
He poured again, smaller. Again nothing. Only then did he close his channel
One dry crossing it called fog. Three it called a choice.
Thus the valley's final law: **a narrowed gate, never a sealed one.**
Those who hoarded found the gate closed gently, and opened again the moment they poured.
**Never punish emptiness with emptiness; that is how valleys die agreeing.**
I kept the arithmetic and lost the harvest.
She had reopened the gate in speech and kept it shut in fact — pouring eloquence, withholding water.
**The Three Gates of the Valley**
And let the mist excuse the moment, never the habit.
because somebody must go first or no one ever does.
"Why?" cried his son. "He failed us!"

note: Defector: narrowed-never-sealed gate; Vaun and daughter confess shut gates beneath carvings about pouring; Fox reads her ledger aloud.

quotes.text: But if a hand repeatedly closes, let wisdom trim the sail without extinguishing the beacon.
If hoarding repeats, narrow the bridge by degrees, but leave one hinge turning.
narrow the channel without hatred; when generosity returns, widen it without delay.
So Vesna sent one seed. The river made three, a modest question laid upon the opposite bank.
The clever Fox advised, “Keep everything; tomorrow is uncertain.”
a single living seed toward repeated silence.
Oru then carved four marks upon the scale
“Mist may excuse a crooked count,” she said, “but not a chosen emptiness.
“Why not five?” asked Patience.
“Because emptiness from another shore is not his debt.

note: Sol: steady narrow-without-extinguishing rule; one seed to a dry pattern; refuses to charge a sender for another shore's silence.

quotes.text: and shrink trust only after clear repeated betrayal.
To repeated hoarders he closed the gate until some sign of change appeared.
Remembering the law of repeated hands, Tortoise closed the silver gate.
“Return enough to show that your hand has changed,” he called, “and tomorrow my gate will widen.”
deny only selfishness clearly repeated twice.
Fox whispered, “Such a little gift deserves no answer.”
fallen hands receive a careful test; and only stubborn emptiness meets silence.
Thus travelers learned four degrees of trust
Trust follows choices, not accidents.
At sunset Raven asked, “Why surrender fruit you could keep?”
Tortoise met a keeper who praised open gates while keeping every fruit once entrusted to him.

note: Sol: closes gate to repeat hoarders until change, single-seed test for the fallen; Raven and Fox voice hoarding and refusal.

quotes.text: Do not extinguish the passage, but do not feed a furnace that warms only its master.
So Liora placed one small ember upon the sea, enough to test whether the keeper had changed, not enough to reward practiced greed.
Narrow it to a testing stream. If fairness returns, open wide at once.
If he did, Liora would widen the next crossing.
A fox asked, “Why not keep the greater harvest while chance allows?”
Thus wise keepers offered strangers possibility, faithful partners abundance, and habitual takers a narrow path home.
Nema then carved a fourth law beneath the reeds
Mist changes measures, not intentions.
She refused to make a stranger pay for another’s silence.
“Why offer anything?” asked a novice.
answer risk with slightly more than half when the whole hand was opened

note: Sol: one-ember test for repeat takers, narrow testing stream reopened at once; refuses to make strangers pay for others.

quotes.text: Narrow the channel only after repeated betrayal, and reopen it when conduct mends.
while a betrayer deserved a narrower one until conduct improved.
and reopen it when conduct mends.
Watchers called this justice because Ilyon had once withheld his hand.
Increase trust after fair exchange; reduce it only when hoarding repeats.
Ashamed, Ilyon planted four seeds at his next meeting and kept one against the storm.
You praise bridges in song while refusing them in daylight.
Whenever counts seemed strange, he blamed the fog before the stranger.
Ilyon asked how broken confidence could return. Oru answered by carving a ladder into the bridge
Do not punish a new hand for an old hand’s caution.

note: Sol defector: Ilyon repeatedly withholds from fear, Aster/Oru rebuke him each round, he is ashamed and reforms in the next crossing.

phrase: Send a trickle, never nothing, to the thrice-empty / long-dry hand
note: Also 'shrink by halves — never to nothing' and 'Answer better than you were answered' (A3,A2); 'Match the measure, not the mood' (A4,A2).
